docs.title: TabPFN Scaling Study on ScAn-Bench
docs.text:
A scaling study of TabPFN on the ScAn-Bench surrogate benchmark, which needs the scan_bench package. Random search samples model and data sizes under a FLOP budget, with a cost_estimator that gives the FLOPs of a configuration before it runs. Each evaluation reports its validation loss, its FLOPs, its number of parameters and data, and the NLL on real data as a downstream performance. scalefm.predict() then fits the scaling law and predicts the loss at larger budgets.

python tabpfn_scan_bench.py

docs.title: LLM Pre-training Scaling Study
docs.text:
A scaling study of small Llama-style language models pre-trained on FineWeb-Edu. Random search samples width, depth, number of tokens and optimization hyperparameters. Each config is trained by its own Slurm job on 1, 2 or 4 GPUs, chosen by a memory probe. scalefm.predict() then fits the scaling law and predicts the loss at larger budgets.

See llm_pretraining/README.md for the full workflow and setup.

docs.title: OpenCLIP Scaling Study
docs.text:
A real-world scaling study: how the contrastive loss of an OpenCLIP model scales with its tower width and depth and the number of LAION image/caption pairs it is trained on, within a FLOP budget. The runs are laid out by Chinchilla approach 1 or 2, or by ScAn, and extrapolated with scalefm.predict. Sampling and training are decoupled so each sampled config -- which can need a very different amount of GPU memory -- is routed to a right-sized Slurm job, with DDP across several GPUs for the largest models.

See vlm_openclip/README.md for the full workflow and setup.

docs.title: Tabpfn scan bench
docs.text:
import logging

from scan_bench import (
    PerformancePredictorType,
    TabPFNBenchmark,
    TabPFNConfig,
    TabPFNTarget,
)

import scalefm

TOTAL_COST = 1e17  
MAX_COST_PER_RUN = 1e16  
TARGET_FLOPS = [1e17, 1e18]

LOSS = TabPFNBenchmark(
    target=TabPFNTarget.VAL_LOSS, predictor_type=PerformancePredictorType.ENSEMBLE_XGB
)
REAL_DATA_NLL = TabPFNBenchmark(
    target=TabPFNTarget.NLL, predictor_type=PerformancePredictorType.ENSEMBLE_XGB
)


def evaluate_pipeline(
    total_cells,
    embedding_size,
    num_layers,
    max_features,
    num_datapoints_max,
    lr,
    effective_batch_size,
):
    config = TabPFNConfig(
        total_cells=total_cells,
        embedding_size=embedding_size,
        num_layers=num_layers,
        max_features=max_features,
        num_datapoints_max=num_datapoints_max,
        lr=lr,
        effective_batch_size=effective_batch_size,
    )
    loss = LOSS.query(config)["predictions"]["mean"]
    real_data_nll = REAL_DATA_NLL.query(config)["predictions"]["mean"]
    return {
        "objective_to_minimize": loss,
        "cost": LOSS.flops(config),
        "downstream_performances": {"real_data_nll": real_data_nll},
        "n_params": LOSS.model_params(config),
        "n_data": total_cells,
    }


def estimate_flops(
    total_cells,
    embedding_size,
    num_layers,
    max_features,
    num_datapoints_max,
    lr,
    effective_batch_size,
):
    config = TabPFNConfig(
        total_cells=total_cells,
        embedding_size=embedding_size,
        num_layers=num_layers,
        max_features=max_features,
        num_datapoints_max=num_datapoints_max,
        lr=lr,
        effective_batch_size=effective_batch_size,
    )
    return LOSS.flops(config)


class TabPFNSpace(scalefm.PipelineSpace):
    total_cells = scalefm.Integer(2**20, 2**35, log=True, is_compute_scaling=True)
    embedding_size = scalefm.Integer(
        4, 256, log=True, log_base=2, is_compute_scaling=True
    )
    num_layers = scalefm.Integer(2, 32, log=True, log_base=2, is_compute_scaling=True)
    max_features = scalefm.Integer(32, 128, log=True, log_base=2)
    num_datapoints_max = scalefm.Integer(128, 512, log=True, log_base=2)
    lr = scalefm.Float(1e-4, 5e-2, log=True)
    effective_batch_size = scalefm.Integer(16, 256, log=True, log_base=2)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
    root_directory = "results/tabpfn_scan_bench"
    scalefm.acquire(
        evaluate_pipeline=evaluate_pipeline,
        pipeline_space=TabPFNSpace(),
        root_directory=root_directory,
        optimizer="random_search",
        cost_estimator=estimate_flops,
        max_cost_per_config=MAX_COST_PER_RUN,
        total_cost_to_spend=TOTAL_COST,
    )
    scalefm.predict(root_directory, TARGET_FLOPS)

docs.title: Analysing Runs
docs.text:
Everything ScaleFM knows about a run lives on disk, in the root_directory you gave to scalefm.acquire(). There are a few ways to look at it:

You want to... Use See how many trials are pending, running, done or crashed, and the best so far scalefm.status Get plots and CSV/text reports of the whole run, at any time scalefm.analyze Have those plots kept up to date while the run is going live_plots=True Follow per-epoch metrics from inside your training loop TensorBoard

docs.title: Trial status: scalefm.status
docs.text:
scalefm.status tells you where a run stands: how many trials are in each state, and the best configuration found so far. It only reads the run; it does not write any files.

CLIPython 
python -m scalefm.status ROOT_DIRECTORY

import scalefm

full_df, short = scalefm.status("ROOT_DIRECTORY", print_summary=True)

full_df has one row per trial (its config, report and metadata) and short summarizes the run as a whole: the same content as summary/full.csv and summary/short.csv.

Using watch

To show the status repeatedly, on unix systems you can use

watch --interval 30 python -m scalefm.status ROOT_DIRECTORY

docs.title: Plots and reports: scalefm.analyze
docs.text:
scalefm.analyze() rebuilds the summary folder of a run from what is on disk: the CSVs and the plots. It does not evaluate anything, so you can call it

  • after a run has finished, in particular one that ran without live_plots=True;
  • while a run is still going, from another process or machine: it writes under the same lock as the workers;
  • after collecting results asynchronously, or after importing trials.
import scalefm

scalefm.analyze("ROOT_DIRECTORY")

docs.title: Which plots?
docs.text: Every figure comes with a CSV of the exact points it shows, so you can re-plot them your own way.

docs.title: Scaling plots
docs.text:
If the runs return a positive cost, ScaleFM draws scaling plots in summary/scaling/, each with a CSV of its points. All of them use log-log axes and mark the Pareto frontier: the runs with the best result for their cost.

Files in summary/scaling/ Plot loss_over_cost.{png,csv} the loss of every run over its training cost, the frontier and the fit of the run's optimizer downstream/<name>_over_cost.{png,csv} the same for each metric in downstream_performances, with a frontier of its own parameters/<name>_over_cost.{png,csv} each number in the config or info_dict that varies, coloured by the loss, with the frontier runs circled pareto_optimal_points.json the runs on the frontier of loss over cost, with their configs

If the runs also return an inference_cost, every plot is drawn over it too (..._over_inference_cost), with frontiers of their own, since a model that is cheap to train can still be expensive to use. Accuracy-like metrics (names containing _acc or recall) are plotted as 1 - value. See the evaluate function for the values to return.

The fit on loss_over_cost is the scaling law the run's optimizer names. The Chinchilla law for the chinchilla optimizer, if the runs return n_params and n_data, and a power law otherwise. scalefm.predict() uses the same one.

docs.title: Prediction plot
docs.text: scalefm.predict(ROOT_DIRECTORY, target_costs) also saves summary/scaling/prediction.png, with its CSVs: the fit extended to the target budgets (left), and the predicted loss after each finished run (right).

docs.title: Live plots during a run
docs.text:
Pass live_plots=True to have the plots redrawn after every evaluated trial as well. Where to pass it depends on how your trials are evaluated: via scalefm.acquire() or scalefm.save_pipeline_results() (see the evaluate function).

Overhead

Each refresh reads every trial and redraws the figures, so it gets slower as the run grows. Next to a training job of a few minutes this is negligible, but for many cheap evaluations, leave live_plots off and call scalefm.analyze() when you want to look.

docs.title: What's on disk?
docs.text:
ScaleFM keeps several human-readable files in the ROOT_DIRECTORY, and a summary folder with reports on the run.

ROOT_DIRECTORY
├── configs
│   ├── config_1
│   │   ├── config.yaml                 # The configuration
│   │   ├── metadata.json               # Its state, worker and timings
│   │   └── report.yaml                 # Its result, once evaluated
│   └── ...
├── summary
│   ├── full.csv                        # One row per trial
│   └── scaling/                        # Scaling plots, if the runs report a cost
├── summary_tb/                         # Scaling data for TensorBoard
├── optimizer_info.yaml                 # The optimizer's configuration
├── optimizer_state.pkl                 # The optimizer's state, shared between workers
└── pipeline_space.pkl                  # The search space

full.csv has every trial's hyperparameters, together with whatever result and cost evaluate_pipeline returned.

docs.title: Scaling data
docs.text:
For runs that report a cost, ScaleFM logs to ROOT_DIRECTORY/summary_tb after every evaluation, with or without live_plots, one step per run:

  • scaling/incumbent/loss: the best loss so far;
  • scaling/frontier/<metric>_over_<cost>: the runs on each Pareto frontier so far, as (trial id, value, cost), for the loss and each downstream metric, over the cost and the inference cost.

The trial ids match summary/full.csv. Logging to TensorBoard never stops a run: if it fails, it only warns and catches up at the next update. TensorBoard shows only 10 text entries per tag by default, so to see the frontier at every step, start it with

tensorboard --logdir ROOT_DIRECTORY/summary_tb --samples_per_plugin text=0

docs.title: Logging your own metrics
docs.text: In ScaleFM we replaced the traditional TensorBoard SummaryWriter with the ConfigWriter to streamline the logging process. This integration enhances the ability to visualize and diagnose hyperparameter optimization workflows, providing detailed insights into metrics and configurations during training.

docs.title: Overview of ConfigWriter
docs.text:
The ConfigWriter serves as a versatile and efficient tool for logging various training metrics and hyperparameter configurations. It seamlessly integrates with the ScaleFM, enabling better visualization and analysis of model performance during hyperparameter searches.

To enable live logging of the incumbent trajectory, use the write_summary_incumbent argument when initializing ConfigWriter.

If a user only wishes to log the incumbent and does not want a specific writer for each configuration (i.e., no other logging in the run pipeline), they should simply trigger the scalefm.tblogger.WriteIncumbent() function in their run pipeline

docs.title: Example Usage
docs.text:
Below is an example implementation of the ConfigWriter for logging metrics during the training process:

import scalefm
# Substitute the TensorBoard SummaryWriter with ConfigWriter from ScaleFM
writer = scalefm.tblogger.ConfigWriter(write_summary_incumbent=True)

for i in range(max_epochs):
    objective_to_minimize = training(
        optimizer=optimizer,
        model=model,
        criterion=criterion,
        train_loader=train_loader,
        validation_loader=validation_loader,
    )

    # Gathering the gradient mean in each layer
    mean_gradient = []
    for layer in model.children():
        layer_gradients = [param.grad for param in layer.parameters()]
        if layer_gradients:
            mean_gradient.append(
                torch.mean(torch.cat([grad.view(-1) for grad in layer_gradients]))
            )

    ###################### Start ConfigWriter Logging ######################
    writer.add_scalar(tag="loss", scalar_value=objective_to_minimize, global_step=i)
    writer.add_scalar(
        tag="lr_decay", scalar_value=scheduler.get_last_lr()[0], global_step=i
    )
    writer.add_scalar(
        tag="layer_gradient1", scalar_value=mean_gradient[0], global_step=i
    )
    writer.add_scalar(
        tag="layer_gradient2", scalar_value=mean_gradient[1], global_step=i
    )

    scheduler.step()

    print(f"  Epoch {i + 1} / {max_epochs} Val Error: {objective_to_minimize} ")

# Logging hyperparameters and metrics
writer.add_hparams(
    hparam_dict={"lr": lr, "optim": optim, "wd": weight_decay},
    metric_dict={"loss_val": objective_to_minimize},
)
writer.close()

docs.title: Visualizing Results
docs.text:
The following command will open a local host for TensorBoard visualizations, allowing you to view them either in real-time or after the run is complete.

tensorboard --logdir path/to/root_directory

This image shows visualizations related to scalar values logged during training. Scalars typically include metrics such as loss, incumbent trajectory, a summary of losses for all configurations, and any additional data provided via the extra_data argument in the tblogger.log function.

This image represents visualizations related to logged images during training. It could include snapshots of input data, model predictions, or any other image-related information. In our case, we use images to depict instances of incorrect predictions made by the model.

The following images showcase visualizations related to hyperparameter logging in TensorBoard. These plots include three different views, providing insights into the relationship between different hyperparameters and their impact on the model.

In the table view, you can explore hyperparameter configurations across five different trials. The table displays various hyperparameter values alongside corresponding evaluation metrics.

The parallel coordinate plot offers a holistic perspective on hyperparameter configurations. By presenting multiple hyperparameters simultaneously, this view allows you to observe the interactions between variables, providing insights into their combined influence on the model.

The scatter plot matrix view provides an in-depth analysis of pairwise relationships between different hyperparameters. By visualizing correlations and patterns, this view aids in identifying key interactions that may influence the model's performance.

docs.title: Cleaning Up Failed Trials
docs.text: The ScaleFM clean command provides a utility to clean up failed, crashed, or corrupted trials from your optimization working directory. By default it resets matched trials to pending, keeping their config so they get re-evaluated on the next run. Pass --delete to remove them entirely instead. This is useful for managing your optimization state and preventing problematic trials from interfering with future optimization runs.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
To reset all non-success stated trials in your optimization directory back to pending:

python -m scalefm.clean --root-dir <root_directory>

If --root-dir is omitted, it defaults to scalefm_results.

docs.title: Dry Run
docs.text:
Preview what would change without making any changes:

python -m scalefm.clean --root-dir <root_directory> --dry-run

docs.title: Cleaning Specific Trial IDs
docs.text:
Reset only specific trials by their IDs (regardless of state):

python -m scalefm.clean --root-dir <root_directory> --trial-ids <trial_id_1> <trial_id_2> <trial_id_3>

Trial IDs are reported in metadata.json within each config directory.

docs.title: Deleting Instead of Resetting
docs.text:
By default, matched trials keep their config on disk and have their state reset to pending (clearing their report), so that a subsequent scalefm.acquire re-evaluates the same configuration rather than sampling a new one. Pass --delete to instead remove the trial directory entirely:

python -m scalefm.clean --root-dir <root_directory> --delete

This can be combined with --dry-run and --trial-ids as usual, e.g.:

python -m scalefm.clean --root-dir <root_directory> --trial-ids 1 2 --delete

docs.title: Python API
docs.text: You can also use the clean functionality programmatically in Python:

docs.title: Reset Failed/Crashed/Corrupted Trials
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path
from scalefm.clean.clean import clean_failed_trials
from scalefm.state.trial import Trial

root_dir = Path("<root_directory>")
stats = clean_failed_trials(
    root_directory=root_dir,
    desired_states=[
        Trial.State.FAILED,
        Trial.State.CRASHED,
        Trial.State.CORRUPTED,
    ],
    dry_run=False,
)

print(f"Reset {stats['total_removed']} trials")

docs.title: Reset Specific Trial IDs
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path
from scalefm.clean.clean import clean_failed_trials

root_dir = Path("<root_directory>")
stats = clean_failed_trials(
    root_directory=root_dir,
    trial_ids=["1", "2"],
    dry_run=False,
)

print(f"Reset {stats['removed']} trials")
print(f"Not found: {stats['not_found']} trials")

docs.title: Deleting Trials
docs.text:
Pass delete=True to remove trials entirely instead of resetting them to pending:

stats = clean_failed_trials(
    root_directory=root_dir,
    desired_states=[Trial.State.FAILED, Trial.State.CRASHED],
    delete=True,
    dry_run=False,
)

docs.title: The evaluate_pipeline function
docs.text: TL;DR Sync: return a dict with at least the loss and the training cost ⟶ ScaleFM records it automatically. Async: call scalefm.acquire(evaluate_pipeline=None, is_async=True) to only sample configurations, launch a job for each, and call scalefm.save_pipeline_results() when the job finishes. Plots: pass live_plots=True to scalefm.acquire() (sync) or to scalefm.save_pipeline_results() (async) to redraw them after every result.

docs.title: 1 Return types
docs.text:
Allowed return When to use Minimal example Dict every evaluation {"objective_to_minimize": loss, "cost": flops} Exception the evaluation failed (raise or return it) raise RuntimeError("diverged")

A plain number is not enough for a scaling study, so any other value, None or a single float included, stops the run with a ValueError. To train the configurations elsewhere (Slurm, k8s, ...), use the asynchronous mode below instead. Only with a cost_estimator passed to scalefm.acquire() may you return just the loss, ScaleFM then adds the estimated cost.

docs.title: 2 Result dictionary keys
docs.text:
key purpose required? objective_to_minimize the loss ScaleFM minimises yes cost the training cost, e.g. FLOPs; also counts towards total_cost_to_spend yes, unless a cost_estimator provides it inference_cost the cost of using the model once, e.g. the FLOPs of one forward pass; the scaling plots are also drawn over it optional n_params the model size; scalefm.predict() fits chinchilla3 and the model size and data on it optional, yes for those fits n_data the amount of training data, e.g. tokens, samples or table cells; as n_params optional, yes for those fits downstream_performances the model's performance on downstream tasks, by name, e.g. {"hellaswag_acc": 0.41}; each gets its own scaling plot optional learning_curve list of intermediate objectives optional info_dict any YAML‑serialisable dict, saved as extra in the trial’s report.yaml optional exception an exception describing a failed evaluation optional 
def evaluate_pipeline(width: int, n_steps: int, learning_rate: float) -> dict:
    ...  # train the model
    return {
        "objective_to_minimize": val_loss,
        "cost": 6 * n_params * n_tokens,  # training FLOPs
        "inference_cost": 2 * n_params,  # FLOPs of one forward pass
        "n_params": n_params,
        "n_data": n_tokens,
        "downstream_performances": {"val_acc": val_acc},
    }

Metrics whose name contains _acc or recall count as higher-is-better and are plotted as 1 - value, so that lower is better in every scaling plot. See Scaling plots for what is drawn from these values.

Live plots When evaluate_pipeline returns its result (sync), the worker records it and refreshes root_directory/summary/. Pass live_plots=True to scalefm.acquire() to also redraw the plots every time: the scaling plots, plus anything the optimizer provides. See Analysing Runs.

docs.title: 3.1 Design
docs.text:
1. scalefm.acquire(evaluate_pipeline=None, is_async=True) only samples configurations. Each one is written to root_directory/configs/config_<id>/config.yaml and stays pending. Passing an evaluate_pipeline together with is_async=True raises a ValueError.
  2. You launch a job for every pending configuration, reading its config.yaml.
  3. The job calls
scalefm.save_pipeline_results(
    user_result=result_dict,
    pipeline_id=pipeline_id,
    root_directory=root_directory,
)

when it finishes. This writes report.yaml and marks the trial SUCCESS / CRASHED.

docs.title: 3.2 Code walk‑through
docs.text:
submit.py – samples a round of configurations and submits a Slurm job for each

from pathlib import Path
import os

import yaml

import scalefm

ROOT_DIRECTORY = Path("path/to/save/results")


class Space(scalefm.PipelineSpace):
    learning_rate = scalefm.Float(1e-5, 1e-1, log=True)
    optimizer = scalefm.Categorical(["sgd", "adam"])


scalefm.acquire(
    pipeline_space=Space(),
    root_directory=ROOT_DIRECTORY,
    is_async=True,  # Only sample, `evaluate_pipeline` stays None
    worker_evaluations_to_spend=4,  # Configurations in this round
)

for config_dir in sorted((ROOT_DIRECTORY / "configs").glob("config_*")):
    script_path = config_dir / "submit.sh"
    if script_path.exists():  # Submitted in an earlier round
        continue
    config = yaml.safe_load((config_dir / "config.yaml").read_text())
    pipeline_id = config_dir.name.removeprefix("config_")
    # Replace CHANGE_ME__PARTITION_NAME with your cluster's partition
    script_path.write_text(f"""#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --time=0-00:10
#SBATCH --job-name=trial_{pipeline_id}
#SBATCH --partition=CHANGE_ME__PARTITION_NAME
#SBATCH --output={config_dir}/%j.out
#SBATCH --error={config_dir}/%j.err

python run_pipeline.py \\
       --learning_rate {config["learning_rate"]} \\
       --optimizer {config["optimizer"]} \\
       --pipeline_id {pipeline_id} \\
       --root_dir {ROOT_DIRECTORY}
""")
    os.system(f"sbatch {script_path}")

Run it again for the next round, it only submits the new configurations.

run_pipeline.py – executed on the compute node

import argparse, json, time, scalefm
from pathlib import Path

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--learning_rate", type=float)
parser.add_argument("--optimizer")
parser.add_argument("--pipeline_id")
parser.add_argument("--root_dir")
args = parser.parse_args()
try:
    # … do heavy training …
    val_loss = 0.1234
    wall_clock_cost = 180  # seconds
    result = {
        "objective_to_minimize": val_loss,
        "cost": wall_clock_cost,
    }
except Exception as e:
    result = {
        "objective_to_minimize": None,
        "cost": None,
        "exception": e,
    }

scalefm.save_pipeline_results(
    user_result=result,
    pipeline_id=args.pipeline_id,
    root_directory=Path(args.root_dir),
)
  • No worker idles while your job is in the queue ➜ better throughput.
  • The job must report cost itself: the cost_estimator passed to scalefm.acquire() only fills in a missing cost for results returned by evaluate_pipeline, not for those saved with scalefm.save_pipeline_results().
  • Pending configurations have no cost yet, so they do not count towards total_cost_to_spend: bound every round with worker_evaluations_to_spend.
  • Crashes inside the job still mark the trial CRASHED instead of hanging.

docs.title: 3.3 Live plots
docs.text:
In async mode the result is recorded by scalefm.save_pipeline_results() in your job, not by the worker, so that is where you ask for the plots to be redrawn:

scalefm.save_pipeline_results(
    user_result=result,
    pipeline_id=args.pipeline_id,
    root_directory=Path(args.root_dir),
    live_plots=True,
)

This refreshes the general plots (the scaling plots) in root_directory/summary/. Optimizer-specific artifacts need the optimizer object, so they are only drawn by scalefm.acquire(..., live_plots=True). To redraw everything once all jobs are done, call scalefm.analyze(root_directory); see Analysing Runs.

docs.title: 3.4 Common pitfalls
docs.text: • When using async approach, one worker, may create as many trials as possible, of course that in Slurm or other workload managers it's impossible to overload the system because of limitations set for each user, but if you want to control resources used for optimization, it's crucial to set desired stopping criteria (e.g total_evaluations_to_spend and/or total_cost_to_spend) when calling scalefm.acquire.

docs.title: 4 Extra injected arguments
docs.text:
name provided when description pipeline_directory always per‑trial working dir (…/trials/<id>/) previous_pipeline_directory always reserved, always None with the built-in optimizers pipeline_id always trial id string you pass to save_pipeline_results

Use them to handle logging and result persistence.

docs.title: 5 Checklist
docs.text:
• [x] Return a dict, or pass no evaluate_pipeline with is_async=True and report from the job.
  • [x] Include cost when using cost budgets.
  • [x] With is_async=True, make sure exactly one call to scalefm.save_pipeline_results happens per configuration.
  • [x] Save checkpoints and artefacts in pipeline_directory.

docs.title: Importing External Trials
docs.text: When optimizing with ScaleFM, you might have evaluations from previous studies that you want to incorporate into your current optimization run. The scalefm.import_trials() function enables seamless integration of externally evaluated configurations into ScaleFM.

docs.title: When to Import Trials
docs.text: There are several scenarios where importing trials is valuable:

docs.title: Scenario 1: Switching Optimization Algorithms
docs.text:
You've already run evaluations with one algorithm (e.g., random search) and want to leverage them with a more sophisticated optimizer (e.g., Bayesian optimization):

# Random search was used for initial exploration
# Now switch to Bayesian optimization with those results
import scalefm

evaluated_trials = [
    ({"learning_rate": 0.001, "batch_size": 32}, scalefm.UserResultDict(objective_to_minimize=0.45)),
    ({"learning_rate": 0.01, "batch_size": 64}, scalefm.UserResultDict(objective_to_minimize=0.38)),
    ({"learning_rate": 0.0001, "batch_size": 16}, scalefm.UserResultDict(objective_to_minimize=0.52)),
]

scalefm.import_trials(
    evaluated_trials=evaluated_trials,
    root_directory="bayesian_study",
    pipeline_space=my_pipeline_space, # need to define pipeline space
    optimizer="bayesian_optimization"
)

# Continue optimization with Bayesian optimization
scalefm.acquire(
    evaluate_pipeline=evaluate_pipeline, # need to define evaluate pipeline
    pipeline_space=my_pipeline_space, # need to define pipeline space
    root_directory="bayesian_study",
    total_evaluations_to_spend=5,  # 5 more evaluations
)

docs.title: Scenario 2: Warm-starting from External Optimization
docs.text:
You've optimized a model using a non-ScaleFM tool and want to continue with ScaleFM:

# Results from your own optimization framework
external_results = [
    ({"model_depth": 5, "learning_rate": 0.01}, scalefm.UserResultDict(objective_to_minimize=0.35)),
    ({"model_depth": 10, "learning_rate": 0.001}, scalefm.UserResultDict(objective_to_minimize=0.32)),
]

scalefm.import_trials(
    evaluated_trials=external_results,
    root_directory="continued_study",
    pipeline_space=my_pipeline_space,
    optimizer="bayesian_optimization"
)

docs.title: Scenario 3: Combining Multiple Optimization Runs
docs.text:
You've performed separate optimization studies and want to merge results:

# Load results from previous run
previous_trials = load_previous_results()  # Your custom loading logic

# Import into new unified study
scalefm.import_trials(
    evaluated_trials=previous_trials,
    root_directory="unified_study",
    pipeline_space=my_pipeline_space,
    optimizer="bayesian_optimization"
)

docs.title: Format 1: Manual Dictionary Format
docs.text:
The simplest format is a list of tuples containing configurations and results:

from scalefm import UserResultDict

evaluated_trials = [
    # (configuration_dict, result_dict)
    (
        {"learning_rate": 0.001, "num_layers": 5},
        UserResultDict(objective_to_minimize=0.45)
    ),
    (
        {"learning_rate": 0.01, "num_layers": 10},
        UserResultDict(objective_to_minimize=0.38)
    ),
]

scalefm.import_trials(
    evaluated_trials=evaluated_trials,
    root_directory="my_study",
    pipeline_space=my_pipeline_space,
    optimizer="bayesian_optimization"
)

docs.title: Result Dictionary Structure
docs.text:
The result dictionary should be a UserResultDict:

scalefm.UserResultDict(objective_to_minimize=0.45)  # Required

# Optional fields:
scalefm.UserResultDict(
    objective_to_minimize=0.45, 
    cost=1000, 
    exception=None, 
    learning_curve=[0.32,0.35],
    info_dict={"something": "whatever information we want to save for this config"},
)

docs.title: Format 2: From Previous ScaleFM Run (Using load_trials_from_pickle)
docs.text:
If your external evaluations were done with ScaleFM previously, use load_trials_from_pickle to easily extract trials:

import scalefm
from scalefm.utils import load_trials_from_pickle

# Load from previous ScaleFM run
evaluated_trials = load_trials_from_pickle(
    root_dir="path/to/old_study"
)

# Import into new study
scalefm.import_trials(
    evaluated_trials=evaluated_trials,
    root_directory="new_study",
    pipeline_space=my_pipeline_space,
    optimizer="bayesian_optimization" # or other optimizer desired for the study
)

docs.title: 1 What optimizer works best for my problem?
docs.text:
For a scaling study, the scaling optimizers build the scaling law into the search: chinchilla splits the compute between model size and data, and carbs searches along the pareto front of objective and cost. To sample a space without assumptions on how it scales, use random_search or grid_search, and bayesian_optimization to find good configurations with fewer evaluations.

Fidelity parameters and priors in the search space are optional, see priors for the optimizers that use them.

docs.title: 2.1 Automatic Optimizer Selection
docs.text:
The algorithms section goes into detail on each optimizer. This chapter focusses on how to select them when using ScaleFM.

✅ = supported/necessary, ❌ = not supported, ✔️* = optional, click for details

Algorithm Priors Model-based Grid Search ❌ ❌ Random Search ✔️* ❌ Complex Random Search ❌ ❌ Bayesian Optimization ❌ ✅ CARBS ✔️* ✅ Chinchilla ❌ ❌

Without an optimizer, scalefm.acquire() uses random_search. Pass "auto" instead to let ScaleFM choose the optimizer based on your search space (or, when continuing a run, to reuse the optimizer it was started with):

  • If it has neither a fidelity nor a prior: bayesian_optimization
  • Otherwise: random_search, sampling around the priors, if there are any
  • If it cannot be converted to a classic search space, e.g. because it has an Operation: complex_random_search

A fidelity is always set to its maximum.

For example, the following chooses an optimizer depending on the pipeline_space passed.

scalefm.acquire(
    evaluate_pipeline=run_function,
    pipeline_space=pipeline_space,
    root_directory="results/",
    total_evaluations_to_spend=25,
    optimizer="auto",
)

docs.title: 2.2 Choosing one of ScaleFM Optimizers
docs.text:
The available optimizers are imported via the scalefm.algorithms module. You can use either the optimizer name or the optimizer class itself as the optimizer argument.

scalefm.acquire(
    evaluate_pipeline=run_function,
    pipeline_space=pipeline_space,
    root_directory="results/",
    total_evaluations_to_spend=25,
    # optimizer specified, along with an argument
    optimizer=scalefm.algorithms.bayesian_optimization, # or as string: "bayesian_optimization"
)

For a list of available optimizers, please refer here.

Interactive tutorial

The ScaleFM demo shows the basic pipeline end to end, with Chinchilla approach 1 and the default random search.

docs.title: 2.3 Hyperparameter Overrides
docs.text:
For users who want more control over the optimizer's hyperparameters, you can input a dictionary with your parameter choices together with the optimizer name.

scalefm.acquire(
    evaluate_pipeline=run_function,
    pipeline_space=pipeline_space,
    root_directory="results/",
    total_evaluations_to_spend=25,
    optimizer=("bayesian_optimization", {"initial_design_size": 5})
)

docs.title: 2.4 Loading Optimizer Information
docs.text:
ScaleFM automatically saves the optimizer metadata (name and configuration) when you run an optimization. You can retrieve this information later using scalefm.load_optimizer_info():

import scalefm

# Load the optimizer info from a previous run
optimizer_info = scalefm.load_optimizer_info("path/to/scalefm_folder")

# Access the optimizer name and configuration
print(f"Optimizer: {optimizer_info['name']}")
print(f"Configuration: {optimizer_info['info']}")

This is useful for:

  • Inspecting what optimizer and settings were used in a previous run
  • Reproducing experiments with the same optimizer configuration
  • Comparing different optimizer settings across runs

Reconstructing a Complete Run

Combine load_optimizer_info() with load_pipeline_space() to fully reconstruct a previous optimization. See Reconstructing and Reproducing Runs for a complete example.

docs.title: 3 Scaling Optimizers
docs.text:
Scaling optimizers build scaling laws into the optimization itself. Instead of finding one good configuration for a fixed setting, they spend a search budget C_search on cheaper configurations and learn how the best configuration changes with cost. From this they predict the best configuration for a larger target cost.

They draw on three arguments of scalefm.acquire(), see estimating the cost of a configuration:

  • cost_estimator: the cost of a configuration, e.g. its FLOPs, known before it is evaluated. It is computed from the parameters marked with is_compute_scaling=True.
  • max_cost_per_config: no configuration estimated to cost more than this is sampled.
  • total_cost_to_spend: the search budget C_search, summed over all evaluations.
Optimizer Approach Supports Install carbs Cost-aware BO along the pareto front of objective and cost Integer and Float parameters, no fidelities see 3.1 CARBS chinchilla Splits compute between model size and data on ISO-FLOP levels Needs cost_estimator and total_cost_to_spend, no fidelities Included

docs.title: 3.1 CARBS
docs.text:
CARBS searches around the pareto front of objective and cost. It starts from a search center and moves to more expensive configurations as it goes, which yields good configurations at every cost, not just one. It needs the cost of every evaluation. That is either the cost returned by evaluate_pipeline or the estimate of the cost_estimator:

scalefm.acquire(
    evaluate_pipeline=run_function,
    pipeline_space=pipeline_space,
    root_directory="results/",
    optimizer=("carbs", {"initial_search_radius": 0.3}),
    cost_estimator=estimate_flops,
    max_cost_per_config=1e12,
)

If the center of the space is too expensive to start from, set search_center_cost_fraction and search_center_shrink_param. The given parameter, e.g. the size of the dataset, is halved until the search center costs at most that fraction of max_cost_per_config.

CARBS wraps an external library, so it is not installed with ScaleFM. It is not on PyPI (the carbs package there is an unrelated project), so install it from GitHub with pip install "carbs @ git+https://github.com/imbue-ai/carbs@8f7fee08658ad567d9dd6b6233247bc37d9962ea".{#carbs-install} It does not keep any files of its own. Its state is rebuilt from the trials in the root_directory whenever a configuration is sampled, so runs can be continued and parallelized like with any other optimizer.

docs.title: 3.2 Chinchilla Guided Scaling
docs.text:
chinchilla follows Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models. It lays out a static list of configurations that grow the model and the amount of data together, to find how a compute budget should be split between the two. The parameters marked with is_compute_scaling=True make up the total scaling parameters and data_parameter_name names the one that sets the amount of data. Every other parameter is drawn at random once and held fixed.

def estimate_params(width: int, layers: int) -> float:
    return ...

scalefm.acquire(
    evaluate_pipeline=run_function,
    pipeline_space=pipeline_space,
    root_directory="results/",
    optimizer=(
        "chinchilla",
        {"data_parameter_name": "n_data", "params_estimator": estimate_params},
    ),
    cost_estimator=estimate_flops,  # (1)!
    max_cost_per_config=1e12,  # (2)!
    total_cost_to_spend=1e14,  # (3)!
)
  1. Required, see the cost_estimator.
  2. Optional. No configuration estimated to cost more than this is laid out.
  3. Required, the configurations are laid out to fit into this budget. worker_cost_to_spend is used if it is not given.
strategy Layout "approach2" (default) Configurations on iso_flop_steps ISO-FLOP levels, up to candidates_per_iso_flop on each "approach1" Every model is trained on data_multipliers times its parameter count

The configurations are laid out on the first ask, and all of them fit into the budget. The run therefore ends with a Grid search exhausted error once every one of them was evaluated, if the budget is not used up before. With live_plots=True, the fitted scaling of parameters and data with the compute is written to the summary folder.

Note

The values of the parameters that are not scaled are drawn when the configurations are laid out, so every worker of a run draws its own.

docs.title: 4 Custom Optimizers
docs.text:
To design entirely new optimizers, you can define them as class with a __call__ method outside of ScaleFM and pass them to the scalefm.acquire() function:

@dataclass
class MyOptimizer:
    space: P
    sampler: Sampler
    encoder: ConfigEncoder

    def __call__(
        self,
        trials: Mapping[str, Trial],
        budget_info: BudgetInfo | None,
        n: int | None,
    ) -> SampledConfig | list[SampledConfig]:
        # Your custom sampling logic here
        ...

The class is then passed to the scalefm.acquire() function just like the built-in optimizers and can be configured the same way, using a dictionary:

scalefm.acquire(
    evaluate_pipeline=run_function,
    pipeline_space=pipeline_space,
    root_directory="results/",
    total_evaluations_to_spend=25,
    optimizer=MyOptimizer,
)

For more details on how to define a custom optimizer see the Optimizer Interface.

To receive the cost_estimator and max_cost_per_config given to scalefm.acquire(), like the scaling optimizers, inherit from ScalingOptimizer:

class MyOptimizer(ScalingOptimizer):
    def __call__(self, trials, budget_info, n=None):
        if self.cost_estimator is not None:
            cost = self.cost_estimator(**config)
        ...

docs.title: Configuring and Running Optimizations
docs.text:
The scalefm.acquire() function is the core interface for running Hyperparameter and/or architecture search using optimizers in ScaleFM. You can find most of the features ScaleFM provides through the API of this function.

This document breaks down the core arguments that allow users to control the optimization process in ScaleFM.

docs.title: Required Arguments
docs.text:
To operate, ScaleFM requires at minimum the following three arguments scalefm.acquire(evaluate_pipeline=..., pipeline_space=..., total_cost_to_spend=...), or, for asynchronous evaluation, scalefm.acquire(is_async=True, pipeline_space=..., total_cost_to_spend=...):

import scalefm

def evaluate_pipeline(learning_rate: float, epochs: int) -> dict:
    # Your code here
    return {"objective_to_minimize": loss, "cost": training_flops}

class ExamplePipeline(scalefm.PipelineSpace):
    learning_rate = scalefm.Float(1e-3, 1e-1, log=True)
    epochs = scalefm.Integer(10, 100)

scalefm.acquire(
    evaluate_pipeline=evaluate_pipeline, # (1)!
    pipeline_space=ExamplePipeline(), # (2)!
    total_cost_to_spend=1e18, # (3)!
    root_directory="path/to/result_dir" # (4)!
)
  1. The objective function, targeted by ScaleFM for minimization, by evaluation various configurations. It requires these configurations as input and should return either a dictionary or a sole loss value as the output.
  2. This defines the search space for the configurations from which the optimizer samples. It accepts a class instance inheriting from scalefm.PipelineSpace or a configSpace.ConfigurationSpace object. For comprehensive information and examples, please refer to the detailed guide available here
  3. The cost budget of the whole study, across all workers, in the unit of the cost that evaluate_pipeline returns, e.g. FLOPs. No new evaluation starts once it is spent. See Budget, how long to run?.
  4. The directory path where the information about the optimization and its progress gets stored. This is also used to synchronize multiple calls to scalefm.acquire() for parallelization.

See the following for more:

  • What kind of pipeline space can you define?
  • What goes in and what goes out of evaluate_pipeline()?

docs.title: Budget, how long to run?
docs.text:
To define a budget, provide total_evaluations_to_spend= to scalefm.acquire(), to specify the number of evaluations after which the whole study (across all workers) stops, and/or total_cost_to_spend= to specify a cost threshold for your own custom cost metric, such as time, energy, or monetary, as returned by each evaluation of the pipeline.

Each of these also has a worker_ variant (e.g. worker_evaluations_to_spend=) that limits only what a single scalefm.acquire() call/worker does.

def evaluate_pipeline(learning_rate: float, epochs: int) -> dict:
    start = time.time()

    # Your code here
    end = time.time()
    duration = end - start
    return {"objective_to_minimize": loss, "cost": duration}

scalefm.acquire(
    total_evaluations_to_spend=10, # (1)!
    total_cost_to_spend=1000, # (2)!
)
  1. Specifies the total number of evaluations a worker is allowed to perform before halting the optimization process.
  2. Prevents the worker from initiating new evaluations once this cost threshold is exceeded. This can be any kind of cost metric you like, such as time, energy, or monetary, as long as you can calculate it. This requires adding a cost value to the output of the evaluate_pipeline function, for example, return {'objective_to_minimize': loss, 'cost': cost}. For more details, please refer here

docs.title: Scaling studies, estimating the cost of a configuration
docs.text:
In a scaling study the cost of a configuration, e.g. its FLOPs, is known before it is evaluated, as it follows from the parameters marked with is_compute_scaling=True. Pass it as cost_estimator= to scalefm.acquire():

class Space(scalefm.PipelineSpace):
    width = scalefm.Integer(64, 1024, log=True, is_compute_scaling=True)
    layers = scalefm.Integer(2, 24, is_compute_scaling=True)
    learning_rate = scalefm.Float(1e-5, 1e-1, log=True)

def estimate_flops(width: int, layers: int) -> float:  # (1)!
    return ...

scalefm.acquire(
    evaluate_pipeline=evaluate_pipeline,
    pipeline_space=Space(),
    cost_estimator=estimate_flops,
    max_cost_per_config=1e12,  # (2)!
    total_cost_to_spend=1e14,  # (3)!
)
  1. Called with the configuration as keyword arguments. A function without **kwargs is only passed the parameters it names.
  2. Optional. Configurations estimated to cost more than this are not sampled.
  3. The estimate is used as the cost of every evaluation that does not report one, so evaluate_pipeline does not have to return a cost for this to work.

If the scaling parameters only take a finite number of values, the costs can instead be given as a JSON file, with one record for every combination of them:

[
  {"config": {"width": 256, "layers": 6},  "cost": 1.2e9},
  {"config": {"width": 256, "layers": 12}, "cost": 2.4e9},
  {"config": {"width": 512, "layers": 6},  "cost": 4.7e9},
  {"config": {"width": 512, "layers": 12}, "cost": 9.4e9}
]

scalefm.acquire(..., cost_estimator="costs.json")

The optimizers that make use of the cost estimate are the scaling optimizers "carbs" and "chinchilla", as well as "bayesian_optimization", "random_search" and "grid_search". Any other optimizer ignores it and logs a warning, the cost of the evaluations is still filled in.

Note

The cost estimator is not stored in the root_directory. Every worker, and every call continuing a run, has to pass the same one.

docs.title: Getting some feedback, logging
docs.text:
ScaleFM will not print anything to the console. To view the progress of workers, you can enable logging through python's logging.basicConfig.

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

scalefm.acquire(...)

Please refer to Python's logging documentation for more information on how to customize the logging output.

docs.title: Live plots
docs.text:
Pass live_plots=True to have ScaleFM redraw the plots in root_directory/summary/ after every evaluated trial: the scaling plots, plus anything your optimizer provides.

scalefm.acquire(..., live_plots=True)

It is off by default, since every refresh redraws the figures. You can always get the same plots later with scalefm.analyze(root_directory). See Analysing Runs.

docs.title: Continuing Runs
docs.text:
To continue a run, all you need to do is provide the same root_directory= to scalefm.acquire() as before, and specify a new stopping criterria(e.g. through total_evaluations_to_spend= and/or total_cost_to_spend=).

def run(learning_rate: float, epochs: int) -> dict:
    start = time.time()

    # Your code here
    end = time.time()
    duration = end - start
    return {"objective_to_minimize": loss, "cost": duration}

scalefm.acquire(
    # enable stoping criteria by specifying new number of evaluation desired.
    total_evaluations_to_spend=50,
)

If a previous run stopped because a worker exhausted its budget, and you restart the run with the same stopping criterion, each worker will again be allowed to spend up to that budget on new evaluations.

As a result, when running multiple workers or restarting a run, the total resource usage may exceed the originally intended global budget. If you have global resource constraints (for example, total cost or total number of evaluations across all workers), you are responsible for tracking and enforcing them externally.

Auto-loading

When continuing a run, ScaleFM automatically loads the search space and optimizer configuration from disk. You don't need to specify pipeline_space= or optimizer= again - ScaleFM will use the saved settings from the original run.

docs.title: Reconstructing and Reproducing Runs
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to inspect what settings were used in a previous run, or reproduce a run with the same or modified settings. ScaleFM provides utility functions to load both the search space and optimizer information:

import scalefm

# Load everything from a previous run
root_dir = "path/to/previous_run"

pipeline_space = scalefm.load_pipeline_space(root_dir)
optimizer_info = scalefm.load_optimizer_info(root_dir)

print(f"Original optimizer: {optimizer_info['name']}")
print(f"Original search space: {pipeline_space}")

# Option 1: Continue the original run (auto-loads everything)
scalefm.acquire(
    evaluate_pipeline=my_function,
    root_directory=root_dir,
    total_evaluations_to_spend=10,  # adjusted new budget
)

# Option 2: Start a new run with the same settings
scalefm.acquire(
    evaluate_pipeline=my_function,
    pipeline_space=pipeline_space,
    root_directory="path/to/new_run",
    optimizer=optimizer_info['name'],
    total_evaluations_to_spend=50,
)

For details on:

  • scalefm.load_pipeline_space() - see Search Space Reference
  • scalefm.load_optimizer_info() - see Optimizer Reference

docs.title: Overwriting a Run
docs.text:
To overwrite a run, simply provide the same root_directory= to scalefm.acquire() as before, with the overwrite_root_directory=True argument.

scalefm.acquire(
    ...,
    root_directory="path/to/previous_result_dir",
    overwrite_root_directory=True,
)

Warning

This will delete the folder specified by root_directory= and all its contents.

docs.title: Getting the results
docs.text:
The results of the optimization process are stored in the root_directory= provided to scalefm.acquire().

Result Directory

The root directory after utilizing this argument will look like the following:

root_directory
├── configs
│   ├── config_1
│   │   ├── config.yaml     # The configuration
│   │   ├── report.yaml     # The results of this run, if any
│   │   └── metadata.json   # Metadata about this run, such as state and times
│   └── ...
├── summary
│   ├── full.csv
│   └── ...                 # Plots, with live_plots=True or scalefm.analyze()
├── optimizer_info.yaml     # The optimizer's configuration
├── optimizer_state.pkl     # The optimizer's state, shared between workers
└── ...                     # Other scalefm files

To check on a run use scalefm.status, and to (re)generate its plots and reports at any time use scalefm.analyze(root_directory). You can also log to TensorBoard from inside your training loop. For more information, please refer to the analyses page.

docs.title: Parallelization
docs.text:
ScaleFM utilizes the file-system and locks as a means of communication for implementing parallelization and resuming runs. As a result, you can start multiple scalefm.acquire() from different processes however you like and they will synchronize, as long as they share the same root_directory=. Any new workers that come online will automatically pick up work and work together to until the budget is exhausted.

Interactive tutorial

The ScaleFM demo runs several workers in parallel on one root_directory, sharing a single FLOP budget.

Worker scriptShell 
# worker.py
scalefm.acquire(
    evaluate_pipeline=...,
    pipeline_space=...,
    root_directory="some/path",
    worker_evaluations_to_spend=100, # (1)!
    continue_until_max_evaluation_completed=True, # (2)!
    overwrite_root_directory=False, #!!!
)
  1. Limits the number of evaluations for this specific call of scalefm.acquire().
  2. Evaluations in-progress count towards worker_evaluations_to_spend, halting new ones when this limit is reached. Setting this to True enables continuous sampling of new evaluations until the total of completed ones meets worker_evaluations_to_spend, optimizing resource use in time-sensitive scenarios.

Warning

Ensure overwrite_root_directory=False to prevent newly spawned workers from deleting the shared directory!

# Start 3 workers
python worker.py &
python worker.py &
python worker.py &

Adding workers scales the throughput of a sweep almost linearly: in our VLM example, 8 workers (one GPU each) run the same 8-evaluation sweep about 7× faster than one.

docs.title: Handling Errors
docs.text:
Things go wrong during optimization runs and it's important to consider what to do in these cases. By default, ScaleFM will halt the optimization process when an error but you can choose to ignore_errors=.

def run(learning_rate: float, epochs: int) -> dict:
    if whoops_my_gpu_died():
        raise RuntimeError("Oh no! GPU died!")

    ...
    return {"objective_to_minimize": loss, "cost": training_flops}

scalefm.acquire(
    ignore_errors=True, # (1)!
)
  1. Continue the optimization process even if an error occurs, otherwise throwing an exception and halting the process.

Note

Any runs that error will still count towards total_evaluations_to_spend.

docs.title: Re-running Failed Configurations
docs.text:
Sometimes things go wrong but not due to the configuration itself. If you want to reset failed or crashed trials so they get re-evaluated, use the scalefm clean command:

python -m scalefm.clean --root-dir <root_directory>

This resets all failed, crashed, and corrupted trials in your working directory back to pending, keeping their configs. To reset specific trials by ID:

python -m scalefm.clean --root-dir results/my_optimization --trial-ids 1 2

You can preview what would change with --dry-run:

python -m scalefm.clean --root-dir <root_directory> --dry-run

If you'd rather remove the trials entirely instead of resetting them, pass --delete.

Once cleaned, you can restart the optimization and workers will pick up from the cleaned state.

For more details on the clean command, see the Cleaning Up Trials documentation.

docs.title: Selecting an Optimizer
docs.text:
By default scalefm.acquire() uses random_search. With optimizer="auto", ScaleFM selects the optimizer based on your pipeline_space=: bayesian_optimization for a space without priors and fidelities, and random_search otherwise, see automatic optimizer selection.

You can also manually select a specific or custom optimizer that better matches your specific needs. For more information about the available optimizers and how to customize your own, refer here.

docs.title: ScaleFM Spaces
docs.text: ScaleFM Spaces provide a powerful framework for defining and optimizing complex search spaces across the entire pipeline, including hyperparameters, architecture search and more.

docs.title: 1. Constructing Hyperparameter Spaces
docs.text:
ScaleFM spaces include all the necessary components to define a Hyperparameter Optimization (HPO) search space like:

  • scalefm.Integer: Discrete integer values
  • scalefm.Float: Continuous float values
  • scalefm.Categorical: Discrete categorical values

Using these types, you can define the parameters that ScaleFM will optimize during the search process. A ScaleFM space is defined as a subclass of PipelineSpace. Here we define the hyperparameters that make up the space, like so:

import scalefm

class MySpace(scalefm.PipelineSpace):
    float_param = scalefm.Float(lower=0.1, upper=1.0)
    int_param = scalefm.Integer(lower=1, upper=10)
    cat_param = scalefm.Categorical(choices=("A", "B", "C"))

Using ScaleFM Spaces

To search a ScaleFM space, pass it as the pipeline_space argument to the scalefm.acquire() function:

scalefm.acquire(
    ...,
    pipeline_space=MySpace()
)

For more details on how to use the scalefm.acquire() function, see the ScaleFM Run Reference.

docs.title: Marking the compute-scaling Parameters
docs.text:
In a scaling study, mark the parameters that set the compute of a configuration, e.g. the model width, the number of layers or the training tokens, with is_compute_scaling=True:

class MySpace(scalefm.PipelineSpace):
    width = scalefm.Integer(lower=64, upper=1024, log=True, is_compute_scaling=True)
    n_layers = scalefm.Integer(lower=2, upper=24, is_compute_scaling=True)
    learning_rate = scalefm.Float(lower=1e-5, upper=1e-1, log=True)

The cost_estimator usually computes the cost of a configuration from them, and Chinchilla lays out its configurations along them.

docs.title: Providing a Fidelity Parameter
docs.text:
You can use scalefm.IntegerFidelity or scalefm.FloatFidelity to mark a parameter that sets how much is spent on an evaluation, e.g. the number of epochs. The optimizers set it to its maximum or treat it like any other parameter, see ignore_fidelity:

# Convenient syntax (recommended)
epochs = scalefm.IntegerFidelity(lower=1, upper=16)
subset_ratio = scalefm.FloatFidelity(lower=0.1, upper=1.0)

# Alternative syntax (also works)
epochs = scalefm.IntegerFidelity(1, 16)

docs.title: Using your knowledge, providing a Prior
docs.text:
You can provide your knowledge about where a good value for this parameter lies by indicating a prior=. You can also specify a prior_confidence= to indicate how strongly you want ScaleFM to focus on these, one of either "low", "medium", or "high":

# Here "A" is used as a prior, indicated by its index 0
cat_with_prior = scalefm.Categorical(choices=("A", "B", "C"), prior=0, prior_confidence="high")

For more details on the optimizers that use priors, see the Priors section.

Adding and removing parameters from ScaleFM Spaces

To add or remove parameters from a PipelineSpace after its definition, you can use the add() and remove() methods. Mind you, these methods do NOT modify the existing space in-place, but return a new instance with the modifications:

space = MySpace()
# Adding a new parameter using add()
larger_space = space.add(scalefm.Integer(lower=5, upper=15), name="new_int_param")
# Removing a parameter by its name
smaller_space = space.remove("cat_param")

docs.title: 3. Constructing Architecture Spaces
docs.text:
Additionally, ScaleFM spaces can describe complex (hierarchical) architectures using:

  • Operation: Define operations and their arguments

Operations can be Callables, (e.g. pytorch objects) which will be passed to the evaluation function as such:

import torch.nn

class NNSpace(PipelineSpace):

    # Defining operations for different activation functions
    _relu = scalefm.Operation(operator=torch.nn.ReLU)
    _sigmoid = scalefm.Operation(operator=torch.nn.Sigmoid)

    # We can then search over these operations and use them in the evaluation function
    activation_function = scalefm.Categorical(choices=(_relu, _sigmoid))

Intermediate parameters

When defining parameters that should not be passed to the evaluation function and instead are used in other parameters, prefix them with an underscore, like here in _layer_size. Otherwise this might lead to unexpected arguments errors.

Operation also allow for (keyword-)arguments to be defined, including other parameters of the space:

    batch_size = scalefm.Categorical(choices=(16, 32, 64))

    _layer_size = scalefm.Integer(lower=80, upper=100)

    hidden_layer = scalefm.Operation(
        operator=torch.nn.Linear,
        kwargs={"input_size": 64,               # Fixed input size
                "output_size": _layer_size},    # Using the previously defined parameter

        # Or for non-keyword arguments:
        args=(activation_function,)
    )

This can be used for efficient architecture search by defining cells and blocks of operations, that make up a neural network. The evaluate_pipeline function will receive the sampled operations as Callables, which can be used to instantiate the model:

def evaluate_pipeline(
    activation_function: torch.nn.Module,
    batch_size: int,
    hidden_layer: torch.nn.Linear):

    # Instantiate the model using the sampled operations
    model = torch.nn.Sequential(
        torch.nn.Flatten(),
        hidden_layer,
        activation_function,
        torch.nn.Linear(in_features=hidden_layer.out_features, out_features=10)
    )

    # Use the model for training and return the validation error and training cost
    model.train(batch_size=batch_size, ...)
    return {"objective_to_minimize": 1 - model.evaluate(...).accuracy, "cost": flops}
Structural Space-compatible optimizers

Currently, ScaleFM Spaces is compatible with these optimizers, which can be imported from scalefm.algorithms:

  • Random Search, which can sample the space uniformly at random
  • Complex Random Search, which can sample the space uniformly at random, using priors and mutating previously sampled configurations
  • Grid Search, for spaces whose only structural choice is a top-level Categorical

docs.title: 4. Constructing Complex Spaces
docs.text:
Until now all parameters are sampled once and their value used for all occurrences. This section describes how to resample parameters in different contexts using:

  • .resample(): Resample from an existing parameters range

With .resample() you can reuse a parameter, even themselves recursively, but with a new value each time:

class ResampleSpace(scalefm.PipelineSpace):
    float_param = scalefm.Float(lower=0, upper=1)

    # The resampled parameter will have the same range but will be sampled
    # independently, so it can take a different value than its source
    resampled_float = float_param.resample()

This is especially useful for defining complex architectures, where e.g. a cell block is defined and then resampled multiple times to create a neural network architecture:

class CNN_Space(scalefm.PipelineSpace):
    _kernel_size = scalefm.Integer(lower=5, upper=8)

    # Define a cell block that can be resampled
    # It will resample a new kernel size from _kernel_size each time
    # Each instance will be identically but independently sampled
    _cell_block = scalefm.Operation(
        operator=torch.nn.Conv2d,
        kwargs={"kernel_size": _kernel_size.resample()}
    )

    # Resample the cell block multiple times to create a convolutional neural network
    cnn = torch.nn.Sequential(
        _cell_block.resample(),
        _cell_block.resample(),
        _cell_block.resample(),
    )

def evaluate_pipeline(cnn: torch.nn.Module):
    # Use the cnn model for training and return the validation error and training cost
    cnn.train(...)
    return {"objective_to_minimize": 1 - cnn.evaluate(...).accuracy, "cost": flops}
Self- and future references

When referencing itself or a not yet defined parameter (to enable recursions) use scalefm.ByName to reference the parameter by its string name:

self_reference = Categorical(
    choices=(
        # It will either choose to resample itself twice
        (scalefm.ByName("self_reference").resample(), scalefm.ByName("self_reference").resample()),
        # Or it will sample the future parameter
        (scalefm.ByName("future_param").resample(),),
    )
)
# This results in a (possibly infinite) tuple of independently sampled future_params

future_param = Float(lower=0, upper=5)

Complex structural spaces

Together, Resampling and operations allow you to define complex search spaces across the whole ML-pipeline akin to Context-Free Grammars (CFGs), exceeding architecture search. For example, you can sample neural optimizers from a set of instructions to train models.

docs.title: Inspecting Configurations
docs.text:
ScaleFM saves the configurations as paths, where each sampling decision is recorded. As they are hard to read, you can retrieve the configuration using scalefm.load_config(), which returns a dictionary with the resolved parameters and their values:

import scalefm

pipeline = scalefm.load_config("Path/to/config.yaml", pipeline_space=SimpleSpace()) # or
pipeline = scalefm.load_config("Path/to/scalefm_folder", config_id="config_0", pipeline_space=SimpleSpace())

# The pipeline now contains all the parameters and their values the same way they would be given to the evaluate_pipeline, e.g. the callable model:
model = pipeline["model"]

docs.title: Loading the Search Space from Disk
docs.text:
ScaleFM automatically saves the search space when you run an optimization. You can retrieve it later using scalefm.load_pipeline_space():

import scalefm

# Load the search space from a previous run
pipeline_space = scalefm.load_pipeline_space("Path/to/scalefm_folder")

# Now you can use it to inspect configurations, continue runs, or analysis

Auto-loading

In most cases, you don't need to call load_pipeline_space() explicitly. When continuing a run, scalefm.acquire() automatically loads the search space from disk. See Continuing Runs for more details.

Reconstructing a Run

You can load both the search space and optimizer information to fully reconstruct a previous run. See Reconstructing and Reproducing Runs for a complete example.

docs.title: Seeding
docs.text:
Seeding is only rudimentarily supported in ScaleFM, as we provide a function to capture the global rng state of Python, numpy and torch. It is not yet possible to seed only ScaleFM internally.

See the Seeding API for the details on how to capture and use this global rng state.

docs.title: What is Bayesian Optimization?
docs.text: Bayesian Optimization/BO is a fundamental optimization technique for finding (local) optima of expensive-to-evaluate functions. The main idea of BO is an interplay of a model (the surrogate function) of the objective function, built from the data collected during the optimization process, and an acquisition function that guides the search for the next evaluation point.

docs.title: The surrogate function
docs.text:
For each dimension of the search space, the surrogate function models the objective function as a Gaussian Process (GP). A GP consists of a mean function and a covariance function, which are both learned from the data. The mean function represents the expected value of the objective function, while the covariance function models the uncertainty of the predictions. The following image shows a GP with its mean function and the 95% confidence interval:

The dashed line represents the (hidden) objective function, while the solid line is the surrogate mean function. The shaded area around the mean function is its confidence interval. Note that the confidence interval collapses where observations have been made and gets large in regions where no data is available yet. (Image Source: Medium.com, Jan 27, 2025)

docs.title: The acquisition function
docs.text:
The acquisition function is the guiding force in BO. From the information contained in the surrogate function, the acquisition function suggests the next evaluation point. It balances the trade-off between exploration (sampling points where the surrogate function is uncertain) and exploitation (sampling points where the surrogate function is promising).

The image shows the surrogate function from before, now with the acquisition function plotted below. The maximum of the acquisition function is the point that will usually be evaluated next. (Image Source: Medium.com, Jan 27, 2025)

There are numerous acquisition functions, with the most popular being Expected Improvement (EI):

  • EI is defined as the expected improvement over the current best observation:
\[EI(\boldsymbol{x}) = \mathbb{E}[\max(0, f(\boldsymbol{x}) - f(\boldsymbol{x}^+))]\]

And Probability of Improvement (PI):

  • PI is defined as the probability that the surrogate function is better than the current best observation:
\[PI(\boldsymbol{x}) = P(f(\boldsymbol{x}) > f(\boldsymbol{x}^+))\]

where \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is the surrogate function and \(f(\boldsymbol{x}^+)\) is the best observation so far.

To read more about BO, please refer to this Bayesian Optimization tutorial or this article on Towards Data Science.

Practical Tips

  • BO can handle expensive-to-evaluate, noisy, high-dimensional and black-box objectives and can be used in the optimization of hyperparameters, neural architectures, and the entire pipeline.
  • It is highly costumizable with many choices for the surrogate and acquisition functions, but even the basic settings work well in many cases.

Info

Therefore, optimizer="auto" chooses BO when the search space has no prior and no fidelity.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text:
Algorithms are the search strategies determining what configurations to evaluate next. In ScaleFM, we provide a few pre-implemented algorithms for scaling studies and offer the possibility to implement custom algorithms. This chapter gives an overview of the algorithms available in ScaleFM.

✅ = supported/necessary, ❌ = not supported, ✔️* = optional, click for details

Algorithm Priors Model-based Scaling-aware Grid Search ❌ ❌ ❌ Random Search ✔️* ❌ ❌ Complex Random Search ❌ ❌ ❌ Bayesian Optimization ❌ ✅ ✔️* CARBS ✔️* ✅ ✅ Chinchilla ❌ ❌ ✅

Scaling-aware optimizers use the cost_estimator of the run, see scaling optimizers.

docs.title: Priors
docs.text: A prior is a value of a parameter that is expected to work well, with a prior_confidence. We discuss how priors can be included in your search space here. random_search samples around them with use_priors=True, and carbs starts its search from them. The other optimizers do not use them.
